## Reflection Symmetry

Mirror symmetry is usually explored across a *reference* **line** (often the vertical or horizontal axis). In contrast to **rotation**, this reference line *lies in the same plane as the 2D shape* under consideration!

How do we define this mathematically? 

A `Reflection Set` would have just two entries: 

$$
\mathbb{R}_{𝑛} = \{ {e,m} \}
$${#eq-reflection-symmetric-group}

because $m^2 = e$; the mirror image of a mirror image is the original object. 

As a matrix, we can write the reflection operation in a similar way compared to rotation: We use a *reference mirror line*, and flip the object to "the other side" of the mirror. We naturally specify that this *reference mirror line* is at an angle $\theta$ wrt to our $X-axis$. So, in 2D, reflection through a line that makes an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis is given by the matrix

$$R_{\text{ref}}(\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos 2\theta & \sin 2\theta \\
\sin 2\theta & -\cos 2\theta
\end{pmatrix}
$${#eq-reflection-matrix}

Special cases:

Reflection across the $x$-axis ($\theta = 0$):
$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Reflection across the $y$-axis ($\theta = 90^\circ$):
$$\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Reflection across the line $y = x$ ($\theta = 45^\circ$):
$$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
These matrices are `orthogonal` with determinant $-1$, which is the algebraic signature of a reflection.


## R example

```{r}
#| label: fig-mirror-symmetry
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-cap: "A shape and its mirror image (outlines + light fill)"
#| echo: false
#| 

base <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 1, 1.5, 1, 0),
  y = c(0, 0.5, 0, -0.5, 0)
)
mirror <- data.frame(x = -base$x, y = base$y)

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = base, aes(x, y), fill = "coral", alpha = 0.25, color = "coral", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = mirror, aes(x, y), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-2, 2), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## p5.js: draw with mirror symmetry

```{=html}
<div id="mirror-sketch"></div>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    if (p.mouseIsPressed) {
      let x = p.mouseX - 200;
      let y = p.mouseY - 200;
      p.stroke(0);
      p.strokeWeight(3);
      p.point(200 + x, 200 + y);
      p.point(200 - x, 200 + y); // vertical mirror
    }
  };
}, document.getElementById("mirror-sketch"));
</script>
<p><em>Click and drag to draw. The sketch mirrors your strokes across the vertical axis.</em></p>
```

::: {.content-hidden}
## Dihedral Symmetry ($D_n$)

Dihedral groups combine rotations of order \( n \) with reflections. These are the symmetries of regular polygons.

## R example: regular pentagon and its symmetries

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "Regular pentagon (D5 symmetry)"

n <- 5
angles <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n + 1)
poly <- data.frame(
  x = cos(angles),
  y = sin(angles)
)

ggplot(poly, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "gold", alpha = 0.6, color = "black") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Dihedral group D5")
```

## p5.js: kaleidoscope-style dihedral drawing

```{=html}
<div id="dihedral-sketch"></div>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let n = 6;
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(400, 400);
    p.background(255);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    if (p.mouseIsPressed) {
      p.translate(200, 200);
      for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        p.push();
        p.rotate(i * p.TWO_PI / n);
        p.stroke(p.random(100, 200), p.random(100, 200), p.random(100, 200));
        p.strokeWeight(2);
        let x = p.mouseX - 200;
        let y = p.mouseY - 200;
        p.line(0, 0, x, y);
        p.line(0, 0, x, -y); // reflection
        p.pop();
      }
    }
  };
}, document.getElementById("dihedral-sketch"));
</script>
<p><em>Click and drag. The sketch applies both rotations and reflections of order 6.</em></p>
```

:::

## Design Notes 

- **Rotational only** ($\mathbb{Z}_{n}$): swirling, pinwheel-like, no mirror lines.
- **Reflection only** ($\mathbb{R}_{𝑛} = \{ {e,m} \}$: bilateral balance (faces, logos, architecture).
- **Dihedral** ($\mathbb{D}_{n}$ ): the most common decorative symmetry (snowflakes, flowers, rose windows, tiles).

These geometric ideas become the constraints we later impose on iterative and random processes.
